notes:
## Entropy
Entropy is a thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the probabilistic distribution of accessible microstates in a system. The term and the concept are used in diverse fields, from classical thermodynamics (where it was first recognized), to the microscopic description of nature in statistical physics, and the principles of information theory. It has far-ranging applications in chemistry and physics, in biological systems and their relation to life, in cosmology, economics, and information systems including the transmission of information in telecommunication.
Entropy is central to the second law of thermodynamics, which states that the entropy of an isolated system left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease with time. As a result, isolated systems evolve toward thermodynamic equilibrium, where the entropy is highest. "High" entropy means that energy is more uniformly distributed or dispersed within a system, while "low" entropy means that energy is more unevenly distributed or concentrated at a specific point or points within a system. A consequence of the second law of thermodynamics is that certain processes are irreversible.

## Laws of thermodynamics
The laws of thermodynamics are a set of scientific laws which define a group of physical quantities, such as temperature, energy, and entropy, that characterize thermodynamic systems in thermodynamic equilibrium. The laws also use various parameters for thermodynamic processes, such as thermodynamic work and heat, and establish relationships between them. They state empirical facts that form a basis of precluding the possibility of certain phenomena, such as perpetual motion. In addition to their use in thermodynamics, they are important fundamental laws of physics in general and are applicable in other natural sciences.
Traditionally, thermodynamics has recognized three fundamental laws, simply named by an ordinal identification, the first law, the second law, and the third law. A more fundamental statement was later labelled as the zeroth law after the first three laws had been established.
The zeroth law of thermodynamics defines thermal equilibrium and forms a basis for the definition of temperature: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

plan.title: Entropy: Why Time Only Runs One Way
plan.description: Entropy measures how spread out energy is within a system. This video explains the second law of thermodynamics and why some processes can never be undone.

beats.narration: Why can you scramble an egg, but never unscramble it? Nothing in the energy books forbids it. Yet it never happens. The answer is a quantity called entropy.

props.title: Why Can't You Unscramble an Egg?
props.subtitle: Entropy and the arrow of time

beats.narration: Think of a tidy desk. There are very few ways to arrange it neatly, and countless ways to make it messy. Left alone, things drift toward the many messy arrangements.
Scientists call each detailed arrangement a microstate. Entropy describes how many microstates a system can access. More ways to arrange the same thing means higher entropy.

props.definition: A thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the distribution of accessible microstates in a system.

beats.narration: In physical terms, high entropy means energy is spread out evenly. Low entropy means energy is concentrated in one place, like a hot spot or a charged battery.
Watch what happens to a hot cup of coffee. It starts with uneven energy. Then energy spreads into the cool room, until everything sits at one temperature, in equilibrium.
This is the second law of thermodynamics. In an isolated system left alone, entropy cannot decrease with time. Systems evolve toward equilibrium, where entropy is highest.

props.text: In an isolated system, entropy never decreases.

beats.narration: A consequence is that certain processes are irreversible. The scrambled egg, the mixed cream, the cooled coffee. Going backward is not impossible by energy rules, just overwhelmingly unlikely.
The idea reaches far beyond kitchens. Entropy appears in chemistry, in living things, in cosmology, in economics, and in how information is sent through telecommunication.

So entropy is not mysterious disorder. It counts the ways energy can be arranged, and nature drifts toward the most likely arrangement. Next time something cools or mixes, you are watching entropy rise.

props.text: Entropy counts the ways energy can spread, and nature favors the most.
